cards.front: Water as the medium for life
cards.back: The first cells originated in water, and water is still the medium in which most life processes (metabolism, transport) happen.
Unequal sharing of electrons in the O–H covalent bonds gives oxygen a partial negative charge (δ−) and each hydrogen a partial positive charge (δ+).
Covalent bonds hold atoms together WITHIN a molecule and are strong; hydrogen bonds form BETWEEN molecules and are weak, but there are so many they matter.
Cohesion = water molecules attracted to EACH OTHER (surface tension, xylem columns). Adhesion = water attracted to a DIFFERENT polar surface (cellulose, glass).
Water moving up a narrow tube, through soil or through plant cell walls: adhesion to the surface plus cohesion pulling the rest of the water along.
Hydrophilic = 'water-loving': polar or charged, dissolves in water (glucose, ions, amino acids). Hydrophobic = non-polar, doesn't dissolve (lipids).

cards.front: Specific heat capacity vs thermal conductivity
cards.back: Specific heat capacity = how much energy it takes to CHANGE temperature. Thermal conductivity = how fast heat MOVES through it. Water is high in both compared with air.
Loon: streamlined body to cut drag from water's high viscosity; buoyancy supports it. Seal: thick blubber to insulate against water's high thermal conductivity.
The monomer of DNA and RNA: one phosphate group + one pentose sugar + one nitrogenous base.
Purines = double-ring bases: adenine and guanine. Pyrimidines = single-ring bases: cytosine, thymine and uracil.
A pairs with T (2 hydrogen bonds) or with U in RNA; G pairs with C (3 hydrogen bonds). Lets one strand act as a template for the other.
The chain of sugars and phosphates joined by covalent (phosphodiester) bonds, formed by condensation reactions, running along each strand.
The two strands of the double helix run in opposite directions: one 5'→3', the other 3'→5'.

cards.front: Three differences between DNA and RNA
cards.back: Strands: DNA double, RNA single. Sugar: deoxyribose vs ribose. Bases: thymine in DNA, uracil in RNA.
mRNA carries the code from DNA to the ribosome; tRNA brings amino acids; rRNA forms part of the ribosome.
With 4 possible bases at each position, a sequence of n bases has 4^n possible combinations (e.g. 3 bases → 64), so DNA can store almost limitless information.
Nearly all organisms use the same codon-to-amino-acid code: evidence that all life shares one common ancestor (LUCA).
1) The cell is the smallest unit of life. 2) All living organisms are made of cells. 3) Cells only come from pre-existing cells.

cards.front: Four structures found in every cell
cards.back: Plasma membrane (controls entry and exit), DNA (instructions), ribosomes (make proteins), cytoplasm (water-based medium for metabolism).
Small (1–10 µm), no nucleus, no membrane-bound organelles: cell wall, plasma membrane, cytoplasm, 70S ribosomes, naked loop of DNA in a nucleoid; maybe plasmids, pili, flagella.
Larger (about 10–100 µm), compartmentalised: nucleus with double membrane and pores, 80S ribosomes, DNA with histones, mitochondria, ER, Golgi, vesicles, cytoskeleton.
Magnification = image size ÷ actual size. Convert both to the same unit first (1 mm = 1000 µm). Magnification has no unit: write ×.

cards.front: Total magnification of a light microscope
cards.back: Eyepiece magnification × objective magnification, e.g. ×10 × ×40 = ×400.
Magnification = how much bigger the image is. Resolution = the smallest distance at which two points can still be seen as separate (how much detail).
Light: lower resolution, specimens can be alive and in colour. Electron (TEM/SEM): much higher resolution, specimens dead, in a vacuum, black and white.

cards.front: Animal vs plant vs fungal cells
cards.back: Walls: none / cellulose / chitin. Chloroplasts: plants only. Vacuole: small and temporary in animals, large and permanent in plants and fungi. Centrioles: animals, not plants.
Skeletal muscle fibre and aseptate fungal hyphae have many nuclei; red blood cells and phloem sieve tube elements have no nucleus.
Metabolism, reproduction, homeostasis, growth, response to stimuli, excretion, nutrition, movement — all shown by single-celled Paramecium.
A species is a group with the same distinguishing physical features (Linnaeus's original idea). Weakness: looks mislead — e.g. males and females, or dog breeds.
A group of organisms that can interbreed to produce fertile, viable offspring. Horse × donkey → mule, which is sterile, so horses and donkeys are separate species.

cards.front: Limits of the biological species concept
cards.back: Can't be used for asexual organisms (bacteria), fossils, populations that never meet, or ring species.
Genus (capital) + species (lowercase), in italics when typed or underlined by hand, e.g. Panthera leo; shorten later to P. leo.
Domain, Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species. Mnemonic: 'Dear King Philip Came Over For Good Soup'.
Discrete: separate categories with nothing in between (blood groups). Continuous: any value in a range (height, mass).
Cells stimulated to divide, stopped at metaphase, stained (G-bands), photographed, arranged in homologous pairs from largest to smallest, sex chromosomes last.
Humans have 46 chromosomes, chimps 48. Human chromosome 2 matches chimp chromosomes 12 + 13 in length and banding, has telomere DNA in the middle and a leftover centromere.
Single-nucleotide polymorphism: a position where one base differs between individuals, found in more than 1% of a population. Any two humans are ~99.9% identical.
Genome size doesn't measure complexity: the Australian lungfish has ~43 billion base pairs and Paris japonica ~149 billion, vs ~3 billion in humans.
Reading an organism's entire genome at once. The Human Genome Project took 13 years and ~$3 billion; by 2020 a genome cost under $600. Used in personalised medicine.
Change in the heritable characteristics of a population over time — or the change in the ratio (frequency) of alleles in a population over time.
Heritable: coded in DNA, passed on (eye colour). Acquired: gained during life, not passed on (gym muscles, suntan). Only heritable change is evolution.
Lamarck: traits acquired by use and disuse are inherited. Darwin: heritable variation already exists, and individuals with favourable variants survive and reproduce more.
It explains and predicts a huge range of observations and is unlikely ever to be falsified, but it can't be formally proven: a 'pragmatic truth'.
Variation → overproduction → competition (selection pressures) → better-adapted individuals survive → they reproduce and pass on alleles → allele frequency changes.
Copies of one allele ÷ total copies of that gene in the population. Count gene copies (2 per individual), not individuals.
Artificial selection: humans breed individuals with desired traits, so the trait becomes more common each generation. Shows heritable change can happen fast.
One species bred for different parts: broccoli (flower buds), cabbage (terminal leaf bud), kale (leaves). Still one species, so this is evolution, not speciation.
Structures in different species that are similar because of common ancestry, even if their functions differ. Produced by divergent evolution.
One proximal bone (humerus/femur) → two distal bones (radius + ulna / tibia + fibula) → wrist/ankle bones (carpals/tarsals) → metacarpals → phalanges.

cards.front: Pentadactyl limb: same bones, different jobs
cards.back: Human hand = tools; bat wing = flight; whale flipper = swimming; horse hoof = galloping; bird wing = flight.
Same function, different evolutionary origin, produced by convergent evolution under similar selection pressures, e.g. dolphin vs shark body; duck vs platypus bill.
Vestigial: reduced, functionless remnants, e.g. whale pelvis (land ancestors). Embryos: all land vertebrates have non-functional pharyngeal slits and a tail.
Mutations build up over time, so fewer differences in DNA or amino acid sequences = more recent common ancestor = more closely related.
Non-coding DNA fastest > gene sequences > amino acid sequences slowest (codon degeneracy). Amino acids for distant taxa, DNA for close relatives.
The splitting of a pre-existing species into two or more. Needs reproductive isolation + differential selection. Gradual change in one lineage is not speciation.
The Congo River (~1.8 million years ago) isolated the ancestors. Chimps competed with gorillas (more aggressive, male-led); bonobos didn't (less aggressive, female-led).
Alleles moving between populations by migration and interbreeding. It keeps populations similar; a barrier stops it, so gene pools diverge.
The variety of life in all its forms, levels and combinations: ecosystem, species and genetic diversity. More biodiversity = a more stable ecosystem.
Richness = the number of different species. Evenness = how equal their numbers are (relative abundance). Same richness can mean very different evenness.
1/D = N(N−1) ÷ Σn(n−1), with n = individuals of each species and N = total. Use n(n−1), not n². Higher = more diverse; maximum ≈ number of species.
High: many niches, even numbers, stable site. Low (close to 1): a few species dominate, often a disturbed site. Same richness but different index = evenness differs.
About 1.2 million described, and perhaps ~7.5 million more undiscovered. Fossils suggest more species are alive now than ever before, because speciation outpaced extinction.
Lumpers group by similarities (fewer species); splitters focus on differences (more species), e.g. giraffes: 1 species traditionally vs 4 in a 2016 genetic study.
Extinction caused by human activity. There have been five mass extinctions; humans are causing a sixth. Only human causes are on the syllabus.
Flightless herbivore up to 3 m tall in New Zealand; only predator Haast's eagle. Polynesian settlers (~1200–1300 CE) overhunted it to extinction within ~100 years.
~250 000 seals in 13 colonies. Docile, so European colonists killed it for oil, blubber and food; prey overfished. Last seen 1952, declared extinct 2008.
Hunted for sport and bounties, captured to hunt blackbuck, grassland and prey lost. Last shot 1947, declared extinct in India 1952: a local extinction.
Direct: humans physically remove it (deforestation, filling wetlands). Indirect: a side-effect from a distance (climate change, pollution, changed tidal flow).
SE Asian rainforest of 500+ hardwood species (a keystone group). Clear-cut for timber then oil palm: ~1% lost per year; orangutans in Borneo endangered.
Seven islands joined by land reclamation from the 1700s; mangroves cleared for housing, roads, ports and salt pans, and damaged by sewage. They protect from storm surges.
IPBES reports and repeated surveys: monitored wildlife populations fell by an average of 73% in 50 years. Evidence must be peer-reviewed and verifiable.
One survey is a snapshot and can't show change. Repeat in the same place with the same method, across many habitats, to show change in richness and evenness.
Pros: huge scale, low cost, public awareness. Cons: misidentification, uneven effort, non-random records near roads and towns, non-standard methods.
Human population growth (overarching) drives over-exploitation, urbanisation, deforestation and land clearance, pollution, invasive species and diseases, and climate change.
An alien species introduced to a new environment that harms the existing food chains, e.g. Burmese python in the Florida Everglades.
Protecting species in their natural habitat: national parks, reserves, anti-hunting laws, monitoring, removing invasives, rewilding. Keeps natural behaviour and the whole habitat.
Protecting species outside their habitat: zoos and captive breeding, botanic gardens, seed and tissue banks. Pros: control, IVF. Cons: habitat not protected, inbreeding.
Rewilding: restoring a damaged ecosystem until it sustains itself (e.g. Yellowstone wolves). Reclamation: restoring land humans used, such as quarries. Both are in situ.
Prioritises species that are both Evolutionarily Distinct and Globally Endangered (IUCN Red List). It informs stakeholders but doesn't decide.
Species have different needs: ex situ rescues critically endangered species and in situ gives them a home to return to, e.g. Arabian oryx, California condor.

quiz.q: Which bonds hold neighbouring water molecules to each other?
quiz.explain: Covalent bonds are inside each molecule; weak hydrogen bonds form between the δ+ H of one molecule and the δ− O of another.

quiz.q: A water strider can stand on a pond mainly because of…
quiz.explain: Cohesion between surface molecules creates surface tension strong enough to hold the insect's weight.

quiz.q: A ringed seal's thick blubber is an adaptation mainly to water's high…
quiz.explain: Water conducts heat away from the body far faster than air, so the seal needs insulation.

quiz.q: A DNA sample is 30% adenine. What percentage is guanine?
How many different sequences can be made from a chain of 3 nucleotides?
quiz.explain: 4 possible bases at each position: 4^3 = 4 × 4 × 4 = 64.

quiz.q: Which base is a pyrimidine found only in RNA?
quiz.explain: Uracil is single-ringed (a pyrimidine) and replaces thymine in RNA.

quiz.q: The near-universal genetic code is evidence that…
choices: all life shares a common ancestor
quiz.explain: If every organism reads codons the same way, the simplest explanation is one common ancestor (LUCA).

quiz.q: A mitochondrion is 45 mm long in a micrograph. Its real length is 3 µm. What is the magnification?
quiz.explain: Convert: 45 mm = 45 000 µm. Magnification = image ÷ actual = 45 000 ÷ 3 = ×15 000.

quiz.q: A chloroplast measures 60 mm in a micrograph at ×12 000. What is its actual length?
quiz.explain: 60 mm = 60 000 µm. Actual = image ÷ magnification = 60 000 ÷ 12 000 = 5 µm.

quiz.q: A scale bar labelled 5 µm is 20 mm long on the image. What is the magnification?
quiz.explain: 20 mm = 20 000 µm. Magnification = 20 000 ÷ 5 = ×4000.

quiz.q: A microscope has a ×10 eyepiece and a ×40 objective. What is the total magnification?
quiz.explain: Total magnification = eyepiece × objective = 10 × 40 = ×400 (multiply, don't add).

quiz.q: Which structure is found in a prokaryotic cell?
quiz.explain: Prokaryotes have smaller 70S ribosomes and no membrane-bound organelles or nucleus.

quiz.q: Fungal cell walls are made of…
quiz.explain: Plants have cellulose walls; fungi have chitin walls; animal cells have no wall.

quiz.q: Which is an example of a cell with MANY nuclei?
quiz.explain: Skeletal muscle fibres and aseptate hyphae are multinucleate; red blood cells and sieve tubes have no nucleus.

quiz.q: A horse and a donkey produce a mule, which is sterile. What does this show?
choices: Horses and donkeys are one species
Horses and donkeys are separate species
The morphological concept is always correct
quiz.explain: The biological species concept needs FERTILE offspring. A sterile hybrid means the parents are different species.

quiz.q: Which is the correct way to write the lion's scientific name (typed)?
quiz.explain: Genus capitalised, species lowercase, in italics when typed (underlined when handwritten).

quiz.q: In a karyogram, chromosomes are arranged…
choices: in homologous pairs, largest to smallest, sex chromosomes last
by the number of genes they carry
in the order they appear in the cell
smallest to largest, sex chromosomes first
quiz.explain: Pairs are matched by length, banding pattern and centromere position, ordered largest to smallest.

quiz.q: Humans have 46 chromosomes and chimpanzees 48 because…
choices: chimps gained two chromosomes from a virus
humans lost a chromosome pair by mutation
two ancestral chromosomes fused to form human chromosome 2
quiz.explain: Chromosome 2 matches chimp chromosomes 12 and 13, and has telomere DNA in its middle where they joined.

quiz.q: The Australian lungfish has about 43 billion base pairs; humans have about 3 billion. This shows that…
choices: lungfish are more complex than humans
genome size is not a measure of complexity
humans have lost most of their genes
quiz.explain: Genome size does not track complexity; only the prokaryote < eukaryote pattern holds.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT an example of evolution?
choices: A bacterial population becoming mostly antibiotic-resistant
Lactase persistence becoming common in a herding population
A man's muscles growing after years of weight training
Maize cobs getting larger over centuries of seed selection
quiz.explain: Muscle from training is acquired, not coded in DNA, so it isn't inherited. Evolution is heritable change in a population.

quiz.q: Which statement is Darwinian rather than Lamarckian?
choices: Giraffes stretched their necks and passed the longer necks on
Giraffes grew longer necks because they needed them
Giraffes born with longer necks survived and reproduced more
Giraffe necks lengthened through use during their lives
quiz.explain: Darwin: selection acts on variation that already exists. 'Needed it' and 'use and disuse' are Lamarck's ideas.

quiz.q: Which pair are homologous structures?
quiz.explain: Bat wings and whale flippers are both pentadactyl limbs from a common ancestor. The others are analogous.

quiz.q: Analogous structures are the result of…
choices: divergent evolution from a common ancestor
convergent evolution under similar selection pressures
quiz.explain: Unrelated species in similar habitats face the same pressures, so similar structures evolve independently.

quiz.q: Species X differs from Y by 2 amino acids in a protein, and from Z by 18. What can be concluded?
choices: X and Y share a more recent common ancestor than X and Z
X and Z are the same species
Y and Z are the most closely related
quiz.explain: Fewer differences = fewer mutations since they diverged = a more recent common ancestor.

quiz.q: Which type of sequence changes FASTEST, making it best for comparing very closely related species?
quiz.explain: Mutations in non-coding DNA don't affect proteins, so they aren't removed by selection and build up fastest.

quiz.q: A single species changes gradually over 2 million years without splitting. This is…
quiz.explain: Speciation needs a pre-existing species to SPLIT. One lineage changing gradually keeps the species count at one.

quiz.q: What separated the ancestors of bonobos and chimpanzees?
quiz.explain: The river was the barrier (reproductive isolation). Gorillas were the different selection pressure on one side.

quiz.q: 100 flowers carry 150 red alleles and 50 white alleles of a colour gene. What is the frequency of the red allele?
quiz.explain: 100 flowers × 2 copies = 200 gene copies. Red = 150 ÷ 200 = 0.75. Don't divide by the number of flowers.

quiz.q: Broccoli was bred from wild Brassica oleracea by selecting for enlarged…
quiz.explain: Broccoli = flower buds, cabbage = terminal leaf bud, kale = leaves. All one species.

quiz.q: Calculate Simpson's reciprocal index (1/D) for a community with species counts 10, 10 and 10.
Calculate Simpson's reciprocal index for species counts 6, 3 and 1.
A mangrove survey finds 20, 18, 15, 12 and 10 individuals of five species. What is 1/D?
Two communities have the same species richness, but P has a higher Simpson's reciprocal index than Q. So P has…
quiz.explain: With richness equal, the only thing left that can raise the index is evenness.

quiz.q: Which is an example of ex situ conservation?
choices: Removing invasive species from a reserve
Storing seeds in a seed bank
quiz.explain: A seed bank keeps genetic material outside the natural habitat. The other three are in situ.

quiz.q: EDGE of Existence prioritises species that are…
quiz.explain: A high EDGE score needs BOTH: few close relatives (ED) and a high IUCN threat level (GE).

quiz.q: What is the overarching cause of the current biodiversity crisis?
quiz.explain: Population growth drives hunting, urbanisation, deforestation, pollution and invasive species. Natural causes aren't on this syllabus point.

quiz.q: Why is the cheetah in India described as a local extinction?
choices: It was never really in India
It was lost from India but survives in Africa and Iran
It is extinct everywhere on Earth
quiz.explain: Last shot in 1947, declared extinct in India in 1952: lost from an area, not from Earth. Cheetahs released in Kuno since 2022.

quiz.q: The Caribbean monk seal was killed by European colonists mainly for…
quiz.explain: Docile seals were killed for oil, blubber and food, and overfishing removed their prey. Declared extinct in 2008.

quiz.q: Why must biodiversity surveys be repeated, using the same method, to give evidence of a crisis?
choices: One survey is a snapshot and cannot show change over time
The first survey is always wrong
quiz.explain: Change needs at least two time points, and the same method means any difference is real, not caused by the method.

quiz.q: After clear-cutting, mixed dipterocarp forest in Southeast Asia is most often replaced by…
quiz.explain: Clear-cut for hardwood timber, then converted to oil palm: about 1% of the rainforest is lost per year.
